lesson.title: Deeper Networks, Bigger Leaps: The Deep Learning Revolution
lesson.summary: Deep learning's modern breakthrough, usually dated to 2012, combined decades old neural network math with large labeled datasets and GPU computing power, launching a wave of advances from image recognition to large language models.
lesson.body:
Deep learning refers to machine learning using artificial neural networks with many layers, often called deep because of that layered structure. Deep neural networks are not a new idea; researchers had experimented with multi layer networks since the 1960s. But the approach fell out of favor for years after Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published a 1969 book called Perceptrons, which mathematically demonstrated significant limitations in the simple, single layer networks common at the time. Although their critique did not apply to networks with multiple layers, it discouraged funding and research interest in neural networks broadly for roughly a decade, contributing to one of the field's AI winters described earlier in this unit.

Deep learning's modern resurgence is usually dated to around 2012, when a deep convolutional neural network called AlexNet, built by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto, won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, a major annual competition for identifying objects in photographs, by a large margin over competing approaches. AlexNet's success depended on three things coming together at once: the backpropagation training method developed decades earlier, a very large labeled dataset of images called ImageNet, and the use of graphics processing units, chips originally designed for rendering video game graphics, to perform the huge number of calculations neural network training requires far faster than general purpose computer processors could. This combination, more than any single new idea, is what many researchers point to as the reason deep learning succeeded when earlier attempts had not.

Progress accelerated quickly after 2012. Researchers developed word embeddings such as word2vec in 2013, techniques that let computers represent the meaning of words as numerical patterns learned from large bodies of text. In 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo, trained using deep learning combined with reinforcement learning, defeated top Go player Lee Sedol, a result many researchers had expected to take years longer given the game's complexity. In 2017, researchers at Google published a paper called Attention Is All You Need, introducing an architecture called the Transformer, which turned out to be extremely effective at processing language and became the foundation for large language models developed over the following years, including the GPT series of models, the first of which was released by OpenAI in 2018, and systems like ChatGPT, launched in November 2022.

The deep learning revolution changed AI from a field mostly of academic and narrow industrial interest into a technology with everyday consumer applications, including image recognition on smartphones, voice assistants, automated translation, and generative tools capable of producing text and images. It also renewed old questions from the earliest years of AI research, about what machines can and cannot understand and how their growing capabilities should be governed, questions the field continues to work through as the technology keeps advancing.
